title: Temporal-Difference Learning
oneLiner: Update your predictions after every single step, using your own guess about what comes next, so learning happens while the episode is still going.

what.html:
Temporal-difference (TD) learning corrects a prediction as soon as the next step reveals a bit more. After each move, the agent compares "what I expected from here" with "the reward I just got plus what I now expect from the next state", and nudges its estimate by a fraction of the difference (the TD error). For choosing actions, SARSA and Q-learning apply the same idea to action values.

Everyday versionDriving home, you estimate 30 minutes. Ten minutes in you hit traffic and now expect 25 more. You don't wait until you arrive to realise your first guess was wrong: you update right away.

why.html:
• No need to wait for the end of an episode, or for episodes to exist at all.
  • No model needed, unlike dynamic programming.
  • Q-learning is the foundation of DQN; TD errors drive actor–critic methods.

how.title: The TD error
how.html: δ = reward + γ × V(next) − V(now). Update V(now) += α × δ. With V = 0.5, reward 1, V(next) = 0.6, γ = 0.9 and α = 0.1, the estimate becomes 0.604.

how.title: TD vs Monte Carlo
how.html: MC waits for the true total (accurate on average, but noisy). TD uses one real step plus a guess (less noisy, but the guess may be off at first). On many problems TD learns faster.

how.title: SARSA: learn what you actually do
how.html: Use the action you really take next: Q += α × (reward + γ × Q(next state, next action) − Q). It learns the value of your behaviour, exploration included.

how.title: Q-learning: learn the best
how.html: Use the best next action instead: Q += α × (reward + γ × max Q(next) − Q). It learns the optimal values even while you explore randomly.

how.title: Average the next action
how.html: Expected SARSA uses the average of the next action values (weighted by how likely each is), removing the randomness of picking one. With a greedy policy it becomes Q-learning.

how.title: Beware the lucky maximum
how.html: The maximum of several noisy estimates is usually too high. Double Q-learning keeps two tables: one picks the best action, the other scores it.

demo.html: A path along a cliff edge. Train both learners: Q-learning finds the shortest path right along the edge but keeps falling off when it explores; SARSA picks a safer route and collects more reward while learning.

example.html:
Same step, three updates. Q(S, A) = 0.5, reward 1, γ = 0.9, α = 0.5. The next state's actions are worth 0.7 (the one taken) and 0.8. SARSA: 0.5 + 0.5 × (1 + 0.63 − 0.5) = 1.065. Q-learning uses the best, 0.8: 1.11. Expected SARSA with 50/50 next actions uses 0.75: 1.0875.

Supplementary If you'll keep exploring after learning (a real robot that sometimes slips), SARSA's caution is a feature, not a flaw.

misunderstandings: They use the current estimate, which may be wrong.
Q-learning learns the values of its behaviour.
It learns optimal values; SARSA learns the behaviour's.
SARSA's safe path is a mistake.
It's optimal for an agent that keeps exploring.
takeaways: Bootstraps like DP, samples like MC; works online.
SARSA is on-policy; Q-learning is off-policy.
Expected SARSA reduces variance; Double Q removes max bias.
Cliff walking: SARSA safe, Q-learning optimal-but-risky while exploring.
thirty: Temporal-difference learning updates estimates after every step toward a bootstrapped target: TD(0) uses δ = R + γV(S′) − V(S) (0.5 → 0.604 in the worked example). It needs no model (like MC) and bootstraps (like DP); its target has lower variance but is biased while V is inaccurate, and batch TD converges to the certainty-equivalence estimate. SARSA updates Q toward R + γQ(S′, A′) using the next action actually taken (on-policy; 1.065 in the worked step); Q-learning uses maxₐ Q(S′, a) and learns q* off-policy (1.11); Expected SARSA averages over the policy and generalises both. Maximisation bias inflates max-based targets; Double Q-learning selects with one table and evaluates with another. On cliff walking SARSA learns a safe path and earns more while exploring; Q-learning learns the optimal edge path but falls off during ε-greedy exploration.
